title: IELTS Writing: Format & Band Descriptors
summary: Two tasks, sixty minutes, and four things the examiner is actually counting. Most candidates lose marks not because their English is weak but because they don't know what's being marked. Here's the whole picture before you write a word.

seo.title: IELTS Writing Format & Band Descriptors Explained | GrowQR
seo.description: IELTS Writing explained: Task 1 vs Task 2, the four band descriptors (Task Response, Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammar), timing and scoring.

objectives: Explain how Task 1 and Task 2 are weighted in your Writing band
Name the four marking criteria and what each rewards
Recognise what separates a band 6 from a band 7 answer
Plan your 60 minutes so Task 2 gets the time it deserves

blocks.html:
You have 60 minutes and two tasks. Task 1 asks for at least 150 words; Task 2 asks for at least 250. It's tempting to write them in order and give each equal effort — that's a mistake. Task 2 is worth roughly twice as much as Task 1 in your final Writing band. Spend your time accordingly.

What changes between Academic and General Training is only Task 1. Academic Task 1 asks you to describe a graph, chart, process or map. General Training Task 1 asks you to write a letter. Task 2 — an essay — is essentially the same for both.

Task 1Task 2
AcademicDescribe a graph, table, chart, process or map (150+ words)Essay responding to an argument or problem (250+ words)
General TrainingWrite a letter — formal, semi-formal or informal (150+ words)Essay responding to an argument or problem (250+ words)
Suggested time20 minutes40 minutes
Weight in band~1/3~2/3

blocks.title: Do Task 2 first if you're a slow writer
blocks.html: There's no rule that says you must write Task 1 first. Because Task 2 carries more marks and needs more thinking, many high scorers write it first while their mind is fresh, then knock out Task 1 in the remaining 20 minutes. Try both orders in practice and keep the one that leaves you calmer.

The four things being marked

Both tasks are scored on the same four criteria, each worth 25% of that task's band. Learn these four names — every improvement you make should target one of them on purpose.

CriterionWhat it rewardsQuick wins
Task Achievement / ResponseAnswering the whole question, with a clear position and developed ideas. (Task 1: covering all the key features / all three bullet points.)Address every part of the prompt; don't go under the word count.
Coherence & CohesionLogical organisation, clear paragraphs, and linking that guides the reader.One idea per paragraph; use a range of linkers, not just "and" and "also".
Lexical ResourceRange and precision of vocabulary, including less common words used correctly.Paraphrase the prompt; avoid repeating the same word; use topic-specific vocabulary.
Grammatical Range & AccuracyA mix of sentence structures with control — complex sentences that stay correct.Combine short sentences with relative clauses and conditionals; proofread for slips.

What a band 7 looks like next to a band 6

The jump from 6 to 7 is where most candidates get stuck. It usually isn't about "harder" English — it's about consistency and control.

CriterionBand 6Band 7
Task ResponseAddresses the task but some parts are underdevelopedAddresses all parts with a clear, developed position throughout
CoherenceOrganised, but linking can be mechanical or overusedLogical progression; a range of cohesion used naturally
Lexical ResourceEnough vocabulary, with some errors in word choiceSome less common vocabulary, with only occasional errors
GrammarA mix of structures; errors are frequent but rarely block meaningA variety of complex structures; the majority of sentences error-free

blocks.title: Under the word count is an automatic penalty
blocks.html: If you write fewer than 150 words (Task 1) or 250 words (Task 2), you lose marks on Task Achievement — before the examiner even weighs your ideas. Learn what 150 and 250 of your words look like on the answer sheet so you never have to count during the exam.

blocks.title: How to spend the hour
items: Read and plan Task 2 — 5 minutes. Underline exactly what the question asks, decide your position, and jot 2 body-paragraph ideas.
Write Task 2 — 30 minutes. Introduction, two developed body paragraphs, conclusion.
Plan and write Task 1 — 20 minutes. For Academic, pick the key features first; for GT, match the tone to the reader.
Proofread — 5 minutes. Hunt your own repeat errors: articles, subject–verb agreement, plurals, word count.

blocks.title: Practise, don't just read
blocks.html: You can't improve writing by reading about it. Head to the Writing Clinic, write a real answer under a prompt, and get an instant estimate of your band across all four criteria — then bring it back up with the checklist there.

faqs.q: How is the IELTS Writing score calculated?
faqs.a: Each task is marked on four criteria — Task Achievement/Response, Coherence & Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range & Accuracy — each worth 25%. Task 2 counts about twice as much as Task 1 toward your overall Writing band.

faqs.q: How long should I spend on each task?
faqs.a: About 20 minutes on Task 1 and 40 minutes on Task 2, because Task 2 is worth roughly twice as much. Include a few minutes to plan and proofread.

faqs.q: What happens if I write fewer than 250 words?
faqs.a: You are penalised on Task Achievement/Response for being under length. Aim comfortably above the minimum — around 160–180 words for Task 1 and 260–290 for Task 2.

faqs.q: Is the Writing test different for Academic and General Training?
faqs.a: Only Task 1 differs: Academic asks you to describe visual data (a graph, chart, process or map), while General Training asks you to write a letter. Task 2 is an essay in both versions.
